title: "Which fin section for an IOM?"
subtitle: "2D CFD of symmetric NACA sections at model-yacht Reynolds numbers, ranked by race time"
author: Kliment Mamykin
date: 2026-10-16
date-format: "D MMMM YYYY"
license: "CC BY"

  title-block-published: "First published"
  title-block-modified: "Updated"
abstract: |
  The fin of an International One Metre (IOM) radio-controlled yacht makes the side force that lets it
  sail upwind. It works at Reynolds numbers of 3×10⁴ to 2×10⁵, where laminar separation bubbles set
  much of the drag. This project compares symmetric NACA sections 6–12\ % thick at chords of 80–100 mm
  with 2D simulations that model laminar–turbulent transition (OpenFOAM, k-ω SST with the
  Langtry–Menter transition model). Sections are ranked not by their drag coefficient but by the race
  time they cost: drag and leeway at equal side force upwind, and drag at zero angle downwind.
  Time-accurate simulations showed that at 4° every section sheds vortices, and that the steady
  solver had overestimated lift there by 4–16\ %. That changed the ranking. On current evidence
  NACA 0007 at 100 mm chord loses the least race time (medium confidence), with NACA 0008 at 100 mm
  as the stiffer alternative. The leading sections are within 1\ % of race time of each other, about
  what keeping the boat clean and fair is worth.
---

## Previous state of the art {#sec-prior}

::: {.callout-note}
## Draft outline
This section is still to be written. The bullets list what it should cover and the sources already
in hand. Each source has to be checked before this page is published. Numbers on this page come from
this project unless a source is cited.
:::

**Fin sections in the IOM class.** What sections and chords do current designs use, and why?
Practitioner writing: Lester Gilbert's design notes on onemetre.net [@gilbert-finforce; @gilbert-vmg]
and Graham Bantock's history of the class [@bantock-iom3]. *To find out:* published comparisons of
fin sections for model yachts, if there are any.

**Low-Reynolds-number aerofoils.** Wind-tunnel polars at Re ≈ 10⁵ [@selig1989], and how laminar
separation bubbles set the drag of thin sections. This project validates against those polars
(@sec-validation).

**Predicting transition.** RANS turbulence models with a transition model [@menter1994; @langtry2009],
and their known weak spot, separation bubbles.

**Surface finish and trips.** Roughness on model yachts [@klaka2022]; boundary-layer trips on
low-Reynolds-number aerofoils [@lyon1997]. The project's research note
[surface-roughness.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/docs/research/surface-roughness.md)
has the details.

**What this project adds.** A ranking by race time rather than drag coefficient, with leeway and the
downwind leg counted, and a check of the steady solutions against time-accurate ones.

## Methodology {#sec-method}

### Simulating a fin section

Each simulation is a 2D slice of the fin: one section at one angle of attack and one boat speed, in
fresh water at 15 °C. It uses OpenFOAM v2512 [@openfoam] with the k-ω SST turbulence model
[@menter1994] and the γ-Re~θ~ transition model of Langtry and Menter [@langtry2009]. The transition
model predicts where the boundary layer stays laminar, separates, reattaches or turns turbulent,
which at these Reynolds numbers decides most of the drag. It needs the turbulence of the incoming
water, Tu. Nobody has measured Tu on a model-yacht pond, so it is a parameter (0.1\ % and 1\ %), not a
constant.

Two solvers are used:

* **Steady** (simpleFoam) finds a flow that doesn't change in time. It is cheap enough to sweep
  hundreds of cases per run, but where the real flow is unsteady its answer can be wrong
  (@sec-transient).
* **Time-accurate** (pimpleFoam) follows the flow in time, here for 30 chord flow-throughs (the time
  the water takes to pass the chord 30 times). The forces are averaged over the last 6. It costs
  8–13 hours per case on one core.

The mesh (@fig-mesh) is a structured C-grid written directly by the project's own generator: 90,112
hexahedral cells, wall-normal grid lines, the first cell sized for y⁺ ≈ 0.5 so that the viscous
sublayer is resolved, and a far field 50 chords away. Doubling the cell count changes drag by 0.1–0.2\ %
at 4° and 0.8–1.7\ % at 6°, and lift by under 0.4\ % (study `mesh-finalists`).

![The medium C-grid for NACA 0007 at 100 mm chord: the whole domain (every 4th grid line), the
section, and the leading edge. Drawn by the same code that writes the simulation
mesh.](_generated/mesh.png){#fig-mesh}

### Validation {#sec-validation}

NACA 0009 at Re = 10⁵ against wind-tunnel data from Princeton [@selig1989]:

![NACA 0009 at Re 10⁵, coarse mesh, Tu 0.1\ %, steady solver. The transition model (used for every
result on this page) gets lift within 6\ % up to 8°; drag is 10\ % high at 4° and 25\ % high at 8°, where
a laminar separation bubble dominates. The fully turbulent model has too much drag at low angles
because it misses the laminar flow.](_generated/validation.svg){#fig-validation}

At upwind angles of 2–5° the transition model is good enough to *rank* sections. Absolute drag is
uncertain by roughly 10–25\ %. Likely causes, roughly in order: the transition model's handling of
separation bubbles; the tunnel's effective turbulence; steady solutions of an unsteady flow at 4°; mesh
resolution; and scatter in the experiment itself.

### From a section to a fin

Each simulation gives a lift and drag coefficient, C~l~ and C~d~. They are scaled to the whole fin,
with span b = 0.36 m below the hull, chord c and dynamic pressure q = ½ρV²:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F &= C_l\, q\, c\, b \\
D &= C_d\, q\, c\, b + \frac{F^2}{2\pi\, q\, e\, b^2}
\end{aligned}
$$

The second term of D is the induced drag of a lifting line, with the hull as a reflection plane and
span efficiency e = 0.9. All fins have the same span, so at equal side force their induced drag is the
same: it adds to the total but doesn't reorder the fins.

### Compare at equal side force

The sails decide how much side force the fin must make, not the fin. So every fin is compared at the
same three forces, the **loads**: what one reference section (0009/80) makes at 2°, 4° and 6°. At
1 m/s these are 1.15 N (light), 6.69 N (working) and 8.33 N (high). For each fin, interpolating along
its lift curve gives the angle it needs, and along its drag curve its drag, at that force
(@fig-equal-force).

![The two steps of the comparison at 1 m/s, Tu 0.1\ %, for the four best fins. Left: the angle each
fin needs to make the load. Right: its drag at that load. Diamonds are the time-accurate 4° points
that replaced the steady ones (dashed); the steady points overestimated lift, so every fin needs more
angle than the steady curves suggested.](_generated/equal-force.svg){#fig-equal-force}

A longer chord makes the same force at a lower angle. The difference in angle is the difference in
**leeway**, because the 3D part of the angle depends on span and force, not chord.

### Race time

Two costs upwind, and one downwind (@fig-course):

![Left: upwind, the boat heads 39° off the true wind [@gilbert-vmg] and slides 3° sideways, so it tracks
at 42° [@gilbert-finforce]. Right: the fin's angle of attack α is the leeway; its side force balances the sails and its
drag slows the boat. Downwind the fin makes no side force and sits at α = 0.](_generated/course.svg){#fig-course}

* **Drag slows the boat.** Extra drag ΔD costs a fraction of the leg's time of
  $$\text{drag loss} = \frac{\Delta D}{V\,\mathrm{d}R/\mathrm{d}V},$$
  where dR/dV is the slope of the boat's total resistance with speed. V dR/dV ≈ 1.35 N at 1 m/s,
  estimated from hull, fin, bulb and rudder friction. At that slope 0.01 N of extra drag costs 0.74\ %
  of the leg.
* **Leeway lengthens the path.** Sailing D metres to windward takes D / cos θ metres of track, with
  θ = 42°. One more degree of leeway costs tan θ · Δα ≈ **1.57\ %** of the leg.
* **Downwind** the fin's drag at 0° counts, at the same boat speed.

With equal time upwind and downwind, a fin's loss is half the sum of the three, measured against the
best fin and averaged over the three loads. The resistance slope is the least certain input, so every
result is also computed with it doubled; tables show both as "×1 / ×2".

An example at working load: 0008/90 is 0.92\ % behind 0007/100. Its extra upwind drag (0.016 N) costs
0.60\ %, its extra 0.36° of leeway 0.29\ %, and its extra downwind drag 0.03\ %. The full method is in
[methodology.md](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/projects/foil2d/methodology.md).

### Robustness

A fin can win on average and still lose badly somewhere. So the ranking is repeated for each
combination of water turbulence (Tu 0.1\ % and 1\ %), resistance slope (×1 and ×2) and solver (steady or
time-accurate 4° points). A fin's **regret** in each case is how far its mean is behind the best fin's;
the largest regret over all cases says how badly the choice could turn out.

## Process and studies {#sec-studies}

The work went in small steps, each a study with a question. Its answer set up the next one
(@tbl-studies).

::: {#tbl-studies}
| when | study | question | answer |
|:----|:----------------|:----------------|:------------------------|
| 11\ Oct | validation | Does the transition model match wind-tunnel data at Re 10⁵? | Well enough to rank sections (@sec-validation). |
| 12\ Oct | selection run 1: 0006, 0009, 0012 × 80, 100 mm; 360 cases | How do thickness and chord trade off? | A thin, short fin wins at light load and a longer chord at high load. At working load the optimum lies between 6\ % and 9\ % thick. |
| 13\ Oct | selection run 2: 0006–0012 × 80, 90, 100 mm; 450 cases | Where between 6\ % and 9\ %? | Thin sections lose at working load because their laminar boundary layer separates at the leading edge. NACA 0012 is out. |
| 13\ Oct | mesh check | Is the mesh fine enough to separate the finalists? | Yes: medium is within 0.2\ % of fine at 4°. |
| 13\ Oct | selection run 3: four finalists at Tu 0.1\ %; 100 cases | Does calmer water change the order? | Calmer water means *more* drag at 4–8°: the laminar bubble grows. |
| 13\ Oct | analysis: leeway and both legs | What does the drag difference cost on the race course? | Counting leeway favours longer chords again; 0008/90 looked like the safest all-rounder. |
| 13\ Oct | selection run 4: 0007/90, 0007/100, 0008/100; 75 cases | Are the thinner, longer sections better still? | Possibly, but the steady 4° solutions oscillated too much to tell. |
| 14\ Oct | time-accurate check 1: 10 cases | Are the oscillating steady points right? | At 6° yes, within 0.5\ %. At 4° every section sheds vortices, and 15 flow-throughs were too few to settle. |
| 15\ Oct | time-accurate check 2: 8 cases continued to 30 flow-throughs | Where do the 4° forces settle? | Lift 4–16\ % below steady. 0007/100 moves to first, 0008/90 to fourth. |
| running | time-accurate check 3: 16 cases | Does that hold at 2°, 6°, and other speeds? | Pending. |

The studies so far. Each has a dated findings log in the repository.
:::

### Steady and time-accurate {#sec-transient}

The steady solver's 4° solutions for the most promising thin sections never settled: their drag
oscillated by up to 22\ %. Time-accurate runs showed why: the flow itself is unsteady. A laminar boundary layer runs to
about a third of the chord, separates, and rolls up into vortices that travel over the rear half.

Getting a reliable time average took two lessons (@fig-force-history):

* **An impulsive start leaves a slow lift build-up.** Lift approaches its final value as the Wagner
  function predicts [@wagner1925; @jones1938]: about 95\ % after 15 flow-throughs, 99\ % after 30. The
  first runs stopped at 15 and were still drifting. They were continued to 30 from where they stopped.
* **Starting from the steady solution settles in about 10 flow-throughs.** The mean is the same either
  way.

![Lift at 4° and 1 m/s. Left: 0007/100 started from rest, continued at 15 flow-throughs; the
dash-dot line is the Wagner build-up scaled to the final mean. Right: 0009/100 started from the steady
solution. Thin lines are the instantaneous lift, which oscillates by about 10\ % as vortices are shed;
the forces are averaged over flow-throughs 24–30 (shaded).](_generated/force-history.svg){#fig-force-history}

The settled means are checked by comparing the two halves of the averaging window: they agree to
within 1.3\ %. Halving the time step changes lift and drag by about 1\ %.

## Visualisations of the findings {#sec-findings}

### What the flow does at 4°

::: {#fig-shedding}
{{< video assets/shedding-video.mp4 >}}

Flow speed and streamlines around NACA 0009 at 4° and Re 10⁵ (time-accurate, coarse mesh). The
laminar boundary layer on the suction side separates and rolls up into vortices that travel over the
rear half and into the wake.
:::

### What the steady solver got wrong

![Lift and drag coefficients at 4° and 1 m/s, steady against time-accurate. Every section makes about
the same time-accurate lift, C~l~ 0.39–0.40; the steady solver spread them from 0.41 to 0.47, and the
thick sections were the most wrong.](_generated/steady-vs-transient.svg){#fig-steady-vs-transient}

At 6° the flow is steady, and the steady drag agrees with the time-accurate one within 0.5\ %. At 4°
the steady points were too optimistic about lift and too pessimistic about drag, and not by the same
amount for every section. That reordered the fins.

### The ranking

![Race-time loss at 1 m/s, Tu 0.1\ %, with the time-accurate 4° points: the mean over the light,
working and high loads (bars, estimated resistance slope) and with the slope doubled (ticks). Less is
better.](_generated/race-time.svg){#fig-race-time}

::: {#tbl-race-time}
{{< include _generated/race-time.md >}}

Race-time loss at 1 m/s, Tu 0.1\ %, % behind the best fin at each load: estimated resistance slope /
doubled. Loads are the side forces of 0009/80 at 2°, 4° and 6°.
:::

0007/100 is first or second in every combination of water turbulence, resistance slope and solver,
and never more than 0.15\ % of race time behind the best mean. The next best, 0007/90, can be up to
0.52\ % behind.

## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

**Recommendation: NACA 0007 at 100 mm chord.** Confidence: medium.

* It loses the least race time at 1 m/s with the time-accurate points: 0.43\ % behind a perfect
  fin-for-every-load on average, against 0.95\ % for 0007/90 and 1.02\ % for 0008/100.
* Its weakest points are mild: 0.8\ % behind 0007/90 in light air, 0.5\ % behind 0008/100 at high
  load.
* Its bending stiffness is about that of 0008/90 (stiffness scales with c·t³, an estimate that ignores
  construction).

**The alternative: NACA 0008 at 100 mm**, if heavy air or stiffness matter more. It is best at high
load and about 50\ % stiffer, and 0.6\ % behind 0007/100 on average.

**How much is at stake.** The four best fins are within 0.9\ % of race time of each other at 1 m/s.
On a 2-lap, 90 m windward–leeward course that is roughly 2–4 boat lengths (an estimate). By
comparison, sanding finer than 400–600 grit gains less than half a boat length, but a dirty, slimy or
unfair hull can cost as much as a poor section choice or more [@klaka2022]. Choose the section, *and*
keep the boat clean and fair.

**Why medium, not high confidence:**

* The time-accurate points are at 1 m/s only, and at 4° only; the 2° and 6° points of most sections
  are still steady ones. Both are being checked.
* The simulations are 2D. Tip, bulb, hull junction and heel are not modelled.
* The resistance slope and the water turbulence are estimates, and the hull and rudder are assumed to
  make no side force.
* The shedding at 4° has not been validated against measurements at these Reynolds numbers.

**What would change it.** In order: time-accurate points at 2° and 6° and at other speeds (running);
a hull resistance curve to replace the estimate; a 3D check of 0007/100 against 0008/100; and the
stiffness of a real fin under the working load.

## Reproducing this {.appendix .unnumbered}

Everything is in [the repository](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd): the simulation setup
(`projects/foil2d/`), every study file, and a findings log per study with the numbers behind each
conclusion. Simulations run in Docker (`uv run iomcfd run foil2d/<study>`) or on Google Cloud Batch.
This page is built from `site/` with Quarto; its charts are drawn from the small data files below,
which `iomcfd site export` copies out of the runs. The code is under the
[MIT licence](https://github.com/kmamykin/iom_cfd/blob/main/LICENSE); the text, figures and data on
this page are under CC BY 4.0. Reference data from other sources keeps its own terms.
